page: Amazon Web Services m1.small is a first-generation general-purpose instance deployed on the Xen hypervisor. It features a single dedicated virtual core derived from an Intel Xeon E5-2651 v2 processor running at 1.8 GHz on the 32-bit i386 architecture. The configuration includes 2.0 GB of system memory, 30 MB of L3 cache, and a bundled 160 GB hard disk drive (HDD) for local ephemeral storage. Hardware acceleration is absent, with no onboard GPU, and baseline network throughput is rated at 0 Gbps.

Benchmark evaluations place the instance in the lowest tiers of contemporary cloud computing performance. The single dedicated core produced a Geekbench single-core score of 490.0 and a multi-core score of 492.0, with PassMark measuring an overall CPU score of 949.92. Memory bandwidth tests registered 8.16 GB/sec for large un-cached read operations and 6.94 GB/sec for writes. The processor lacks modern vector extensions such as AVX, AVX-512, and FMA, although hardware AES encryption is present. Operational throughput benchmarks reflect these constraints, yielding 0.46 million Redis SET operations per second and 1.09 GB/sec in static web serving throughput.

The primary architectural tradeoffs of the m1.small stem from its legacy i386 instruction set, limited single-core processing capabilities, and reliance on magnetic spinning disk storage rather than solid-state media. From a resource perspective, it represents a legacy baseline tier suitable primarily for running lightweight 32-bit legacy software, minimal background utilities, low-traffic static web servers, or archival testing environments that require compatibility with older generation x86 environments.
